solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Empty fajita, very hot on the outside, in the main

indicators.note: an emptied word has lost its contents, so only its outermost letters remain
something on the outside wraps around whatever sits within it

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
searing heat is intense heat

explanation.surface: A diner complains of a hollow fajita, scorching outside, eaten somewhere out in the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Empty' removes the filling of the wrap, just as it would in the kitchen. 'The main' is an old poetic name for the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Seafaring describes travel or work on the ocean, and 'the main' is a literary term for the high seas.

clue.text: Short, stout person rowing up to the half-way mark

indicators.note: stopping at the half-way mark means the second half of the word is dropped

blocks.note: a row is a noisy quarrel, so rowing is squabbling

explanation.surface: A chunky rower pulls hard until reaching the midpoint of the course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rowing' suggests oars but means quarrelling (rhymes with 'cow'); SQUABBLING has ten letters, and the first five give SQUAB.
explanation.definitionFit: Squab is a dated word for a short, plump person, as well as a young pigeon.

clue.text: Periodically cheers up, given what you may be reading now

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the letters are read from bottom to top

blocks.note: ta is British informal thanks, like cheers

blocks.clueFragment: what you may be reading now
blocks.note: the clue appears in The Times newspaper

explanation.surface: Someone occasionally brightens up while reading the paper in front of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The self-reference works because this puzzle is printed in The Times. 'Cheers' in Britain can mean thanks, as can TA.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean occasionally or from time to time, happening now and then rather than continuously.

clue.text: Appeal after copper stops working case

indicators.note: one element coming after another sets their order in the chain
a stopper plugs a hole, so this pair sits inside another word

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
SA is short for sex appeal
something working is active

explanation.surface: A police officer's appeal halts a legal case that was in progress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' and 'case' suggest a police story; case is grammatical. SA for sex appeal is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: The accusative is a grammatical case marking the direct object of a verb, as in Latin or German.

clue.text: Briefly with or without Mary?

blocks.note: surface reading: a quick question about whether a woman called Mary is coming along
setter's reading: a common phrase for briefly still means briefly whether or not the name Mary is on its end

explanation.surface: A host asks, in passing, whether Mary will be joining the party.
explanation.walkthrough: IN SUMMARY means briefly; drop MARY from its end and IN SUM still means briefly, so the answer works with or without Mary.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are used to introduce a short concluding statement, meaning to put it concisely.

clue.text: Venue for sports fan getting snack food

blocks.note: a sports ground, such as a football or cricket ground
a nut is an enthusiast, as in a fitness nut

explanation.surface: A supporter at the stadium buys something to eat during the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sports fan' looks like one unit, but the split falls between 'sports' and 'fan'.
explanation.definitionFit: A groundnut is another name for a peanut, a popular salty snack.

clue.text: Might one be a surrogate father?

definitions.text: Might one be a surrogate father?

blocks.note: surface reading: a man who stands in as a parent, perhaps in a surrogacy arrangement
setter's reading: a Father is a priest, and a temporary substitute for a priest or doctor has a Latin-derived title

explanation.walkthrough: 'Father' pulls towards family; here it is a clergyman, and the stand-in who covers his duties is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A locum is a professional, usually a doctor or clergyman, temporarily filling in for another.

clue.text: Story including Fitzgerald’s opening sentence

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter
to include something is to take it inside

blocks.note: a story can be an untruth
the first letter of the name

explanation.surface: A tale that includes the first line of a Scott Fitzgerald novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening sentence' reads as a literary phrase, but the two words split apart: 'opening' selects, 'sentence' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A life sentence is imprisonment for the remainder of one's natural days, often called simply life.

clue.text: Bread and a little butter, with spicy drink going around

indicators.note: going around something means encircling it

blocks.note: a pat is a small portion of butter
chai is spiced Indian tea

explanation.surface: An Indian meal: flatbread with butter, and spiced tea served alongside.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface reads like a menu, so it is easy to take 'Bread and a little butter' together.
explanation.definitionFit: A chapati is an unleavened flatbread from South Asian cooking, made from wholemeal flour.

clue.text: Where hammer and anvil are extremely tough taken from Tolkien’s realm

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters
what is taken from something is removed from it

blocks.note: the fictional world of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: The blacksmith's forge in Tolkien's world is a tough place, with hammer and anvil at work.
explanation.walkthrough: Hammer and anvil sound like a forge, but they are the malleus and incus, tiny bones of the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: The malleus (hammer) and incus (anvil) are ossicles located in the cavity behind the eardrum.

clue.text: Company that delivers, bagging credit increases

indicators.note: to bag something is to put it inside a sack

blocks.note: UPS is the American parcel delivery firm
buying on tick is British slang for buying on credit

explanation.surface: A courier firm takes on more debt as its business grows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Credit' suggests finance to match the company, but it is British slang: buying 'on tick' is buying on credit.
explanation.definitionFit: An uptick is a small rise, especially in a price or figure, so upticks are increases.

clue.text: Casual worker missing work to begin with

indicators.note: placing something to begin with puts it at the front of the chain

blocks.note: someone off is away from their job
a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: A temporary labourer who skipped work right from the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casual worker' looks like one phrase for a temp; 'Casual' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: An offhand manner is careless or nonchalant, showing little concern or attention.

clue.text: Live entertainment not primarily what a crossword may provide?

indicators.note: not primarily means without what comes first, so the opening letter is lost

blocks.note: to be is to exist or live
amusement is entertainment

explanation.surface: Live shows are not the main thing a crossword offers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Live entertainment' reads as a single phrase for concerts, but 'Live' is a verb here. The question mark admits the definition is playful.
explanation.definitionFit: A tricky puzzle leaves the solver puzzled and confused, which is bemusement, with a nod to amusement too.

clue.text: Booty from large house picked up

indicators.note: to pick up a sound is to hear it, so the word is judged by ear

blocks.note: a hall is a large country house

explanation.surface: Loot is collected from a stately home by burglars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' fits the burglary picture as taking the loot, but it signals hearing. In British speech the two words sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A haul is a quantity of stolen goods or plunder taken in one go.

clue.text: Kind of green plan to recycle

blocks.note: a chart is a plan or map
to recycle is to use again

explanation.surface: An environmentally friendly scheme for recycling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' and 'recycle' suggest ecology; here green is a colour and 'recycle' is not an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Chartreuse is a yellowish-green shade named after the French liqueur of that colour.

clue.text: Not firm figure in French radio, perhaps

blocks.note: un is French for one
a radio is an example of a set, a receiving apparatus

explanation.surface: An uncertain personality broadcasting on French radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' looks like a person but means a number.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unset, like jelly or concrete, has not yet hardened into a solid state.

clue.text: Not in country club with tree outside for all to see

indicators.note: being outside something means surrounding it

blocks.note: the United Nations is an organisation whose members are countries
the poplar is a tall tree
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing

explanation.surface: Someone excluded from the golf club, with a tree blocking the view of everyone watching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country club' suggests golf, but the club is one of nations. U, a British film rating, means suitable for all ages.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in is to be fashionable or accepted, so not in means disliked or out of favour.

clue.text: Alcohol and some cocaine — last bit of crack

blocks.note: punch is a mixed alcoholic drink
a line is a portion of cocaine laid out to snort

explanation.surface: A drug-fuelled night: booze, cocaine, and the final hit of crack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' continues the drugs story, but it is a wisecrack, and 'last bit' is not a letter selector.
explanation.definitionFit: A crack is a joke, and the punchline is its final part that delivers the humour.

clue.text: Privileged person with clout drunkenly punching twit

indicators.note: a drunk staggers about, so these letters lurch into a new order
a punch drives into its target, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
prat is British slang for an idiot

explanation.surface: An influential rich man, drunk, hits a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clout' fits the power theme and also means a blow, but it is only fodder. PRAT is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A plutocrat is someone whose power and status derive from great wealth.

clue.text: European arriving at chamber for event

indicators.note: arriving at something places one element right up against the next

blocks.note: a Pole is a native of Poland
a vault is an underground chamber

explanation.surface: A delegate arrives at the parliamentary chamber for a function.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Event' sounds like a gathering; it is a contest in athletics.
explanation.definitionFit: The pole vault is a track and field discipline in which athletes clear a high bar using a flexible pole.

clue.text: Mathematician climbing mountain in pretty fabric

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means reading from bottom to top
being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: an alp is a high mountain
lace is a delicate decorative fabric

explanation.surface: A scholar scales a peak, patterned on a delicate cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climbing' suits the mountain in the surface, but in a down entry it sends the letters upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre-Simon Laplace was a French scholar famous for work in probability, celestial mechanics and the Laplace transform.

clue.text: One getting into flash car?

indicators.note: whatever gets into something ends up inside it

blocks.note: an ace is the one in a suit of cards or on a die
a Rolls-Royce, abbreviated RR, is the classic showy car

explanation.surface: Someone climbs into a showy luxury vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a driver climbing into a Rolls might well be a speed merchant, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A racer is a competitive driver, someone who gets behind the wheel of a fast car to compete.

clue.text: Perverse creature who might pinch twirling girl attending many parties

indicators.note: something twirled is spun round so it faces the other way

blocks.note: a crab nips with its pincers
a debutante is a young society woman doing the rounds of balls and parties

explanation.surface: An awkward character who might grope a dancing girl at a round of parties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinch' suggests stealing or groping, but it points to claws. DEB is short for debutante, a young woman introduced to high society.
explanation.definitionFit: Crabbed means bad-tempered or contrary, and can also describe cramped, hard-to-read handwriting.

clue.text: Man with issue twice a year

blocks.note: p.a. is per annum, Latin for a year, written two times

explanation.surface: A man who has a problem that crops up every six months.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' is offspring, not a problem.
explanation.definitionFit: Issue is a formal word for children, so a man with issue is a father.

clue.text: Group receiving direction before start of Long March

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter
one thing before another fixes their order in the chain
to receive is to take something in

blocks.note: an order is a direction or instruction
the first letter of the word
a band is a group

explanation.surface: A troop is given orders before setting off on the Long March in China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long March' evokes Mao's retreat, but March is the definition, a noun for frontier land.
explanation.definitionFit: A march is an old term for a frontier region between two territories, as in the Welsh Marches.

clue.text: Call e.g. ChatGPT capital

blocks.note: to dub someone is to give them a name
ChatGPT is an example of artificial intelligence

explanation.surface: Someone declares a chatbot to be a major asset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' could be money or a letter; here it is a city.
explanation.definitionFit: Dubai city is the seat of government of the emirate of Dubai in the United Arab Emirates.

clue.text: Day with stormy rain one’s spent in Algeria, say

indicators.note: a storm throws things around, so these letters are tossed into a new order

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for day
taken as written

explanation.surface: A day of heavy rain spent on holiday in North Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spent' suggests time passed on holiday, but it means paid out as money.
explanation.definitionFit: The dinar is the official currency of Algeria, and 'say' marks it as one example among several countries.

clue.text: Character from Jerusalem I name in support of peace!

indicators.note: in a down entry, something in support holds up what sits above, so it comes below

blocks.note: sh is a call for quiet
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A figure from Jerusalem announces themselves as backing peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' looks like a person, but it is a letter of an alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Shin is a letter of the Hebrew alphabet, the script used in Jerusalem.

clue.text: Hide eastern articles in both hands

indicators.note: being in something means placed inside it

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for eastern
a and the are the indefinite and definite articles
L and R stand for left and right

explanation.surface: Someone conceals goods from the East, clutching them in both hands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' reads as a verb, but it is the noun for an animal skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Leather is tanned animal skin, and a hide is an animal's skin, raw or processed.

clue.text: The spirit of Henry IV, say

blocks.note: first meaning: an American whiskey made mainly from corn
second meaning: a member of the French royal house that Henry IV founded

explanation.walkthrough: Henry IV here is the king of France, not the English king of Shakespeare's play; 'The spirit' sounds like his character or ghost.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a corn whiskey from Kentucky and the dynasty that ruled France from Henry IV onwards.

clue.text: Some perfumier he interested in eau de Cologne locally

indicators.note: some of a phrase is only part of it, so the letters run within the words

blocks.note: running across the word boundaries

explanation.surface: A perfume maker shows interest in the famous scented water from Cologne.
explanation.walkthrough: Eau de Cologne is a scent, but read literally it is 'water of Cologne', the river flowing through that city, named as Germans name it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cologne stands on the Rhine, whose German name is used by local people there.

clue.text: Henry quits Asian bank, perhaps he goes in last

indicators.note: whoever quits leaves, so a letter departs from the phrase

blocks.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
a Thai person is from Thailand in Asia
a bank is a lender

explanation.surface: Henry resigns from an Asian bank, perhaps being the last to join.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the batting order runs from openers to the weakest batsmen, who go in last.
explanation.definitionFit: A tail-ender is a lower-order cricket batsman, usually a bowler, who bats near the end of the innings.
